title: Gems and Ores
objective: After this level you can explain what makes a mineral a gem and what makes a rock an ore worth mining.
summary: A gem is a mineral prized for beauty, durability and rarity; ruby and sapphire are both corundum. An ore is rock whose minerals can be mined at a profit.

cards.headline: A ruby and a blue sapphire are the same mineral.
cards.body: Same recipe, different color. So what turns a mineral into a gem? And what turns a rock into something worth digging up?

cards.headline: What makes a gem
cards.body: A gemstone is a mineral prized for three things: beauty, durability and rarity. Beauty comes from color, clarity and the way it plays with light. Durability means it keeps its polish through years of handling, which is where hardness helps: remember Level 3's diamond at 10? A few gems break Level 2's rules entirely. Pearl, coral and amber aren't minerals at all.

cards.fact: Ruby and sapphire are both corundum, a mineral made of aluminum oxide.
cards.context: Pure corundum is colorless. A trace of chromium turns it red, and it's a ruby. Iron and titanium turn it blue, and it's a sapphire. At 9 on the Mohs scale, corundum is second in hardness only to diamond, which helps both gems last.

cards.headline: What makes an ore
cards.body: An ore is a natural collection of minerals that can be mined and sold at a profit. That's an economic test, not a geological one: every ore deposit is a mineral deposit, but not the other way round. Whether a deposit pays depends on how rich and big it is, the cost of mining and shipping, and market prices. Level 3's red-streaked hematite is a key iron ore.

options.rationale: Most ores are metal sources, like iron.
